entries.title: Japanese at a glance
body: Japanese puts the verb at the end of the sentence (subject, object, verb) and marks the role of each phrase with a small particle after it, so word order before the verb is fairly free.
Nouns have no plural and no gender, and there are no articles. Verbs do not change for person: {食べます} means I, you, she or they eat, and the subject is often left out when context makes it clear.
Three scripts are mixed in ordinary text: hiragana, katakana and kanji.

examples.e: (I / we / they) eat. The subject is understood.

entries.title: Hiragana, katakana and kanji
body: {Hiragana} writes native words, grammatical endings and particles. {Katakana} writes loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia and emphasis. {Kanji} carry the meaning of most nouns and verb stems.
Each kana stands for one mora, so there are 46 basic signs in each kana set. Children learn about 1,000 kanji in primary school; the official list for everyday use (jōyō kanji) has 2,136.

examples.e: I drink coffee. (kanji · hiragana · katakana · hiragana)

entries.title: On-yomi and kun-yomi
body: Most kanji have two kinds of reading. The {on-yomi} came from Chinese and is mostly used in compounds of two or more kanji. The {kun-yomi} is the native Japanese word and is used when the kanji stands alone or is followed by kana.
Dictionaries often write on-yomi in katakana and kun-yomi in hiragana.

entries.title: Okurigana
entries.body: Kanji write the stem of a verb or adjective and hiragana write the part that changes. Those trailing kana are called okurigana. They also tell you which reading of the kanji is meant.

examples.t: 食{べる} · 食{べない} · 食{べた}

entries.title: Morae, long vowels and small っ
body: Japanese rhythm counts morae: every kana is one beat of equal length. A long vowel takes two beats and a small {っ} adds a held, silent beat before the next consonant. Length changes meaning, so hold them.
{ん} is a beat of its own too: こんにちは is five beats, ko-n-ni-chi-wa.

examples.t: おばさん / お{ばあ}さん

entries.title: Pitch accent
entries.body: Japanese has no stress accent. Instead each word has a pattern of high and low pitch, and some words that are spelled the same in kana differ only in pitch. The patterns below are standard Tokyo Japanese.

examples.e: chopsticks (high then low) / bridge (low then high)

entries.title: Particles は (wa) and が (ga)
body: {は} marks the topic: what the sentence is about, often something already known. {が} marks the grammatical subject, and puts the focus on it: new information, or the answer to who or what.
Question words such as 誰 (who) and 何 (what) take が, never は, when they are the subject. Note that the particle は is pronounced wa.

examples.e: As for me, I'm a student.
Tanaka came. (Tanaka is the new information.)
Elephants have long trunks. (As for elephants, the trunk is long.)

entries.title: を, に, で, へ, と, の
entries.body: Each particle follows the word it marks. These six cover most everyday sentences. を is pronounced o and へ is pronounced e when they are particles.

head: Particle
Marks
Example
rows: パンを食べる · eat bread
destination, time, indirect object, place where something is
学校に行く · go to school; 七時に · at seven
place where an action happens, means
図書館で読む · read at the library; バスで · by bus
東京へ行く · head for Tokyo
友達と話す · talk with a friend
私の本 · my book; 日本語の先生 · Japanese teacher

entries.title: これ, それ, あれ, どれ
entries.body: Pointing words come in sets by distance: {ko-} near the speaker, {so-} near the listener, {a-} away from both, and {do-} for the question.

entries.title: Questions with か
entries.body: Add {か} to the end of a statement to make it a question; the word order does not change. In polite speech the question mark is optional, because か already does the job. Casual speech often drops か and uses rising intonation.

entries.title: Verb groups
body: Every verb's dictionary form ends in -u. {Ichidan} (ru-) verbs end in -iru or -eru and simply drop る. {Godan} (u-) verbs change their final kana across the a-i-u-e-o row. Only two verbs are fully irregular: {する} (do) and {来る} (come).
Some verbs ending in -iru / -eru are godan anyway, such as 帰る (go home), 入る (enter), 走る (run) and 知る (know).

entries.title: Polite and plain forms
entries.body: Use the polite です / ます forms with people you don't know well, at work and with anyone older. Use the plain forms with friends and family, and inside longer sentences.

entries.title: The て-form
body: The て-form joins actions (and then…), makes requests with ください, and builds -ている (doing now, or a lasting state). Ichidan verbs swap る for て. Godan verbs follow the ending of the dictionary form.
The one exception: 行く (go) becomes 行って.

head: Ending
Becomes
Example
rows: 買う → 買って · 待つ → 待って · 帰る → 帰って
飲む → 飲んで · 遊ぶ → 遊んで · 死ぬ → 死んで

examples.t: ちょっと待{って}ください。

entries.title: い-adjectives and な-adjectives
body: {い-adjectives} end in い and conjugate themselves: drop い and add くない (not), かった (was), くなかった (wasn't). {な-adjectives} behave like nouns: they take な before a noun and use です / だ for tense.
いい (good) is irregular: よくない, よかった.

head: い: 高い (expensive)
な: 静か (quiet)
rows: 静かじゃなかったです

entries.title: Numbers and counters
body: Sino-Japanese numbers: いち, に, さん, よん (し), ご, ろく, なな (しち), はち, きゅう (く), じゅう. Larger numbers are built as in Chinese: 二十 (20), 百 (100), 千 (1,000), 万 (10,000).
Things are counted with a counter word chosen by their shape or kind, and sounds often change at the join (いっぽん, さんぼん, ろっぽん).

head: Counter
Used for
rows: ひとつ · ふたつ · みっつ
ひとり · ふたり · さんにん
いっぽん · にほん · さんぼん
いちまい · にまい · さんまい
いっぴき · にひき · さんびき
いっさつ · にさつ · さんさつ

examples.t: ありがとうございます

examples.e: Said after eating: thank you for the meal.

examples.t: よろしくお願いします
examples.e: Nice to meet you. I'm counting on you.

entries.title: Keigo: respectful language
body: Beyond です / ます (teineigo, the polite level) Japanese has {sonkeigo}, which raises the person you talk about, and {kenjōgo}, which lowers yourself. Shop staff, receptionists and business email use them constantly.
Several common verbs have their own respectful and humble words.

head: Plain
Respectful (their action)
Humble (my action)
rows: 行く · 来る · いる

entries.title: There is: ある and いる
entries.body: Use {いる} for people and animals (things that move by themselves) and {ある} for objects, plants and events. Place に first, then the thing with が.

examples.t: 机の上に本が{あります}。
examples.r: tsukue no ue ni hon ga arimasu
examples.e: There is a book on the desk.
There is a dog in the park.

examples.t: 明日テストが{あります}。
examples.e: There is a test tomorrow. (events use ある)

entries.title: Wanting: -たい and ほしい
entries.body: Add {-たい} to the ます stem to say you want to do something; it then conjugates like an い-adjective. Use {ほしい} for wanting a thing. Both describe your own feelings; for other people, add -がっている or say it indirectly.

examples.t: 新しい靴が{ほしい}です。

entries.title: Giving and receiving
entries.body: Japanese has three verbs for giving and receiving, chosen by direction. {あげる}: I (or my side) give outward. {くれる}: someone gives to me or my side. {もらう}: I receive, with the giver marked by に or から. They also attach to て-forms for doing favours.

examples.t: 友達に花を{あげました}。
友達が花を{くれました}。
友達に花を{もらいました}。
examples.e: I got flowers from my friend.

examples.t: 手伝って{くれて}ありがとう。
